pairs.question: Stemmata quid faciunt?
pairs.answer: nobilitas sola est atque unica uirtus.
pairs.derivation: The satire opens with the author's own rhetorical question 'Stemmata quid faciunt?' (what do family trees accomplish?), line 1. After a long run of further rhetorical questions (quid prodest, quo, cur...) about the uselessness of pedigree, the author states his own resolving thesis at line 20: 'nobilitas sola est atque unica uirtus.' Question and answer are each a single contiguous source sentence; the intervening rhetorical questions are not included in either field. Stripped the inline verse numbers (5, 10, 15, 20) and the bracketed editorial lines.

pairs.question: his ego quem monui?
pairs.derivation: Author poses a genuine interrogative about whom he has been admonishing ('his ego quem monui?', line 39) and immediately answers it himself: 'tecum mihi sermo, Rubelli Blande' (my discourse is with you, Rubellius Blandus). Both fields are verbatim and contiguous across the 39-40 line break; the inline verse number 40 mid-passage is stripped. The answer stops at the full stop; what follows ('tumes alto Drusorum stemmate...') elaborates the rebuke.
